title: Conditional and Null Operators
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behavior of conditional and null operators in C#.
Identify the relevant operand types, evaluation rules and result types.
Read and explain original C# code that demonstrates the lesson concepts.
Predict deterministic program output and identify common mistakes.
Compile and execute a small .NET 10 console example to verify the result.

understand.concept: The conditional operator (condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse) selects one of two expressions. The null-coalescing operator ?? returns its left operand when it is non-null, otherwise it evaluates and returns the right operand. The null-coalescing assignment operator ??= assigns a fallback only when the left operand is null. The null-conditional operators ?. and ?[] safely access members or indexers and produce null when the receiver is null. These operators help express fallback and optional access without verbose branching.
understand.whyItMatters: They make fallback values and optional data handling concise while preserving null safety.
understand.analogy: The conditional operator is a two-way signpost; null-coalescing is a backup plan used only when the preferred value is missing.
understand.analogyLimit: These operators do not replace validation. A fallback may hide missing data if the application should instead report an error.

explain.narrative:
## Conditional operator

`condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse` evaluates the condition and then evaluates only the selected expression. The two result expressions must have a compatible type.

## Null-coalescing operators

`left ?? fallback` returns `left` when it is not null; otherwise it evaluates the fallback. `??=` assigns a value only if its left operand is null. These operators are useful for optional configuration and default values.

## Null-conditional access

`customer?.Name` returns null if customer is null; otherwise it accesses Name. `items?[0]` safely performs an indexer access when items is null. Chained null-conditional access can prevent null-reference exceptions, but the application may still need to decide what missing data means.

Examples target .NET 10 and C# 14.

questions.prompt: Why should a developer understand operand types?
questions.answer: Types affect which operation is selected and what result is produced.
